claim: Layer four receives the densest bottom up sensory inputs in the neocortex.
source: Layer four receives the densest bottom up sensory inputs, while layers 2/3 and 5 receive top down inputs that may convey predictive information.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about neocortical organization in the abstract.

claim: Layers 2/3 and 5 receive top down inputs that may convey predictive information.
source: Layer four receives the densest bottom up sensory inputs, while layers 2/3 and 5 receive top down inputs that may convey predictive information.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about neocortical organization in the abstract.

claim: Martinotti cells gate top down input by inhibiting the apical dendrites of pyramidal cells in layers 2/3 and 5.
source: A subset of cortical somatostatin (SST) neurons, the Martinotti cells, gate top down input by inhibiting the apical dendrites of pyramidal cells in layers 2/3 and 5, but it is unknown whether an analogous inhibitory mechanism controls activity in layer 4.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract, citing prior work.

claim: It is unknown whether an analogous inhibitory mechanism controls activity in layer 4.
source: A subset of cortical somatostatin (SST) neurons, the Martinotti cells, gate top down input by inhibiting the apical dendrites of pyramidal cells in layers 2/3 and 5, but it is unknown whether an analogous inhibitory mechanism controls activity in layer 4.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap motivating the study.

claim: Martinotti cells connect with layers 2/3 and 5 in mouse barrel cortex.
source: Martinotti cells connect with layers 2/3 and 5, whereas non-Martinotti cells connect with layer 4.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract, supported by circuit mapping experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: Non-Martinotti cells connect with layer 4 in mouse barrel cortex.
source: Martinotti cells connect with layers 2/3 and 5, whereas non-Martinotti cells connect with layer 4.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract, supported by circuit mapping experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: Martinotti cells and non-Martinotti cells are genetically distinct SST subtypes.
source: Using high precision circuit mapping, in vivo optogenetic perturbations, and single cell transcriptional profiling, we reveal complementary circuits in the mouse barrel cortex involving genetically distinct SST subtypes that specifically and reciprocally interconnect with excitatory cells in different layers
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract, supported by single-cell RNA sequencing data.

claim: Parallel SST subnetworks could independently regulate the balance between bottom up and top down input by enforcing layer-specific inhibition.
source: By enforcing layer-specific inhibition, these parallel SST subnetworks could independently regulate the balance between bottom up and top down input.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Excitatory principal cells in each cortical layer differentially encode and process sensory information.
source: Excitatory principal cells (PCs) in each layer differentially encode and process sensory information (Feldmeyer, 2012; Harris and Shepherd, 2015), due in part to the fact that they receive different external inputs.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to prior work.

claim: Bottom-up sensory inputs primarily enter L4.
source: 'Bottom-up' sensory inputs primarily enter L4, while 'top down' inputs target PCs in supragranular and infragranular layers.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about cortical organization.

claim: Top down inputs target PCs in supragranular and infragranular layers.
source: 'Bottom-up' sensory inputs primarily enter L4, while 'top down' inputs target PCs in supragranular and infragranular layers.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about cortical organization.

claim: SST-expressing interneurons shape sensory coding through lateral and recurrent inhibition.
source: Dendrite-targeting somatostatin (SST)-expressing interneurons are well known for shaping sensory coding through lateral and recurrent inhibition, and for gating top-down input by regulating dendritic spiking and synaptic plasticity (Adesnik et al., 2012; Kim, 2016; Kvitsiani et al., 2013; Makino and Komiyama, 2015; Urban-Ciecko and Barth, 2016; Kato et al., 2017; Veit et al., 2017; Adesnik, 2017).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with multiple citations.

claim: SST neurons gate top-down input by regulating dendritic spiking and synaptic plasticity.
source: Dendrite-targeting somatostatin (SST)-expressing interneurons are well known for shaping sensory coding through lateral and recurrent inhibition, and for gating top-down input by regulating dendritic spiking and synaptic plasticity (Adesnik et al., 2012; Kim, 2016; Kvitsiani et al., 2013; Makino and Komiyama, 2015; Urban-Ciecko and Barth, 2016; Kato et al., 2017; Veit et al., 2017; Adesnik, 2017).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with multiple citations.

claim: SST neurons send and receive synaptic connections with neurons across multiple cortical layers.
source: While it is well established that SST neurons send and receive synaptic connections with neurons across multiple cortical layers (Apicella et al., 2012; Jiang et al., 2015; Jiang et al., 2013; Anastasiades et al., 2016; Otsuka and Kawaguchi, 2009; Yoshimura and Callaway, 2005; Kapfer et al., 2007), it is unclear whether SST circuits impact all layers in a global manner, or if instead they selectively control specific layers, which could have profound impacts for cortical computation.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with multiple citations.

claim: It is unclear whether SST circuits impact all layers in a global manner or selectively control specific layers.
source: While it is well established that SST neurons send and receive synaptic connections with neurons across multiple cortical layers (Apicella et al., 2012; Jiang et al., 2015; Jiang et al., 2013; Anastasiades et al., 2016; Otsuka and Kawaguchi, 2009; Yoshimura and Callaway, 2005; Kapfer et al., 2007), it is unclear whether SST circuits impact all layers in a global manner, or if instead they selectively control specific layers, which could have profound impacts for cortical computation.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap motivating the study.

claim: Inhibitory neurons interconnect with excitatory cells densely and non-selectively.
source: Studies which have examined connectivity of SST cells (Fino and Yuste, 2011) and GABAergic interneurons more generally (Bock et al., 2011; Scholl et al., 2015; Hofer et al., 2011; Packer and Yuste, 2011) have found that inhibitory neurons interconnect with excitatory cells densely and non-selectively, which has led to the emerging hypothesis that excitatory circuits are overlaid by a 'blanket of inhibition'.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from prior studies with citations.

claim: The emerging hypothesis is that excitatory circuits are overlaid by a 'blanket of inhibition'.
source: Studies which have examined connectivity of SST cells (Fino and Yuste, 2011) and GABAergic interneurons more generally (Bock et al., 2011; Scholl et al., 2015; Hofer et al., 2011; Packer and Yuste, 2011) have found that inhibitory neurons interconnect with excitatory cells densely and non-selectively, which has led to the emerging hypothesis that excitatory circuits are overlaid by a 'blanket of inhibition'.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis from the literature with citations.

claim: The SST population is highly heterogeneous.
source: However, the SST population is highly heterogeneous (Urban-Ciecko and Barth, 2016; Yavorska and Wehr, 2016) and can be divided into multiple subgroups of cells which exhibit distinct electrophysiological, morphological, genetic (Tasic et al., 2016), and in vivo functional properties (Kim, 2016; Kvitsiani et al., 2013; Muñoz et al., 2017; Ma et al., 2010; Reimer et al., 2014; Nakajima et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with multiple citations.

claim: The SST population can be divided into multiple subgroups with distinct electrophysiological, morphological, genetic, and in vivo functional properties.
source: However, the SST population is highly heterogeneous (Urban-Ciecko and Barth, 2016; Yavorska and Wehr, 2016) and can be divided into multiple subgroups of cells which exhibit distinct electrophysiological, morphological, genetic (Tasic et al., 2016), and in vivo functional properties (Kim, 2016; Kvitsiani et al., 2013; Muñoz et al., 2017; Ma et al., 2010; Reimer et al., 2014; Nakajima et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with multiple citations.

claim: Some SST subgroups target their axons to different laminar domains.
source: Intriguingly, some of these subgroups target their axons to different laminar domains (Ma et al., 2006; Muñoz et al., 2014; Nigro et al., 2018), and it has been hypothesized that subgroups of SST cells might be specialized to differentially modulate the activity of specific layers (Muñoz et al., 2017), perhaps by forming distinct subnetworks.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: It has been hypothesized that subgroups of SST cells might be specialized to differentially modulate the activity of specific layers.
source: Intriguingly, some of these subgroups target their axons to different laminar domains (Ma et al., 2006; Muñoz et al., 2014; Nigro et al., 2018), and it has been hypothesized that subgroups of SST cells might be specialized to differentially modulate the activity of specific layers (Muñoz et al., 2017), perhaps by forming distinct subnetworks.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis from prior work with a citation.

claim: 93% of L5 GIN cells are Martinotti cells.
source: Consistent with prior data, the anatomy and intrinsic physiology of L5 GIN cells demonstrated that they are MCs (41/44; 93%; Figure 1a and Figure 1—figure supplement 1) (Wang et al., 2004; Kawaguchi, 1993; Fanselow et al., 2008; Kinnischtzke et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on anatomical and physiological characterization, with citations to prior work.

claim: 91% of neurons in the X94 line are non-Martinotti cells.
source: By similar analyses, neurons in the X94 line were non-Martinotti cells (32/35; 91%), which formed a dense axonal plexus in L4 rather than L1 (Figure 1a, Figure 1—figure supplement 2) and exhibited quasi-fast-spiking electrophysiological phenotypes (Figure 1b, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on anatomical and physiological characterization.

claim: X94 line neurons form a dense axonal plexus in L4 rather than L1.
source: By similar analyses, neurons in the X94 line were non-Martinotti cells (32/35; 91%), which formed a dense axonal plexus in L4 rather than L1 (Figure 1a, Figure 1—figure supplement 2) and exhibited quasi-fast-spiking electrophysiological phenotypes (Figure 1b, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on anatomical characterization shown in figures.

claim: X94 line neurons exhibit quasi-fast-spiking electrophysiological phenotypes.
source: By similar analyses, neurons in the X94 line were non-Martinotti cells (32/35; 91%), which formed a dense axonal plexus in L4 rather than L1 (Figure 1a, Figure 1—figure supplement 2) and exhibited quasi-fast-spiking electrophysiological phenotypes (Figure 1b, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on electrophysiological characterization shown in figures.

claim: The X94 line labels only ~15% of SST cells in L5.
source: While the X94 line labels only ~15% of SST cells in L5 (Ma et al., 2006), additional recordings from L5 SST-TdT cells suggested that the X94 line subsamples the NMC population (consistent with a previous report) since 30–40% of recorded L5 SST cells exhibited an NMC phenotype (Figure 1—figure supplement 1c–g).
evidence: This is stated as a finding with a citation to prior work.

claim: 30–40% of recorded L5 SST cells exhibited an NMC phenotype.
source: While the X94 line labels only ~15% of SST cells in L5 (Ma et al., 2006), additional recordings from L5 SST-TdT cells suggested that the X94 line subsamples the NMC population (consistent with a previous report) since 30–40% of recorded L5 SST cells exhibited an NMC phenotype (Figure 1—figure supplement 1c–g).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on recordings from SST-TdT cells.

claim: L5 MCs primarily innervated layers 1, 2/3 and 5.
source: Aligning biocytin reconstructions of L5 MCs and NMCs revealed that these two populations have strikingly complementary vertical profiles of neurite density: MCs primarily innervated layers 1, 2/3 and 5, and NMCs primarily innervated L4 and the L5/L6 border (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on biocytin reconstructions shown in Figure 1c.

claim: NMCs primarily innervated L4 and the L5/L6 border.
source: Aligning biocytin reconstructions of L5 MCs and NMCs revealed that these two populations have strikingly complementary vertical profiles of neurite density: MCs primarily innervated layers 1, 2/3 and 5, and NMCs primarily innervated L4 and the L5/L6 border (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on biocytin reconstructions shown in Figure 1c.

claim: L5 MCs and NMCs have strikingly complementary vertical profiles of neurite density.
source: Aligning biocytin reconstructions of L5 MCs and NMCs revealed that these two populations have strikingly complementary vertical profiles of neurite density: MCs primarily innervated layers 1, 2/3 and 5, and NMCs primarily innervated L4 and the L5/L6 border (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on biocytin reconstructions shown in Figure 1c.

claim: L5 MCs receive inputs from L5 and L2/3.
source: Remarkably, we found that L5 MCs and NMCs receive inputs from highly specific and largely non-overlapping sources. MCs, but not NMCs, frequently received excitatory input from either upper L5, L2/3, or from both L2/3 and L5, but received little input from L4 or L6, broadly consistent with prior studies (Apicella et al., 2012; Jiang et al., 2015; Anastasiades et al., 2016; Kapfer et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on optogenetic circuit mapping, with citations to prior studies.

claim: L5 MCs received little input from L4 or L6.
source: Remarkably, we found that L5 MCs and NMCs receive inputs from highly specific and largely non-overlapping sources. MCs, but not NMCs, frequently received excitatory input from either upper L5, L2/3, or from both L2/3 and L5, but received little input from L4 or L6, broadly consistent with prior studies (Apicella et al., 2012; Jiang et al., 2015; Anastasiades et al., 2016; Kapfer et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on optogenetic circuit mapping, with citations to prior studies.

claim: NMCs received strong input from L4 and/or the L5B/L6 border.
source: In contrast, NMCs received strong input from L4 and/or the L5B/L6 border (Figure 1e,f; input from L4 and L6 was 62 ± 7% of total input for n = 14 NMCs versus 25 ± 3% for n = 15 MCs; p=6.5 · 10−10; two sample T-test; see also Figure 1—figure supplement 3) but relatively little input from L2/3 and L5.
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on optogenetic circuit mapping shown in figures.

claim: Input from L4 and L6 was 62 ± 7% of total input for n = 14 NMCs versus 25 ± 3% for n = 15 MCs (p=6.5 · 10−10).
source: In contrast, NMCs received strong input from L4 and/or the L5B/L6 border (Figure 1e,f; input from L4 and L6 was 62 ± 7% of total input for n = 14 NMCs versus 25 ± 3% for n = 15 MCs; p=6.5 · 10−10; two sample T-test; see also Figure 1—figure supplement 3) but relatively little input from L2/3 and L5.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study based on optogenetic circuit mapping.

claim: NMCs received relatively little input from L2/3 and L5.
source: In contrast, NMCs received strong input from L4 and/or the L5B/L6 border (Figure 1e,f; input from L4 and L6 was 62 ± 7% of total input for n = 14 NMCs versus 25 ± 3% for n = 15 MCs; p=6.5 · 10−10; two sample T-test; see also Figure 1—figure supplement 3) but relatively little input from L2/3 and L5.
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on optogenetic circuit mapping.

claim: L5 MCs and NMCs receive distinct and complementary patterns of excitatory innervation.
source: Thus, L5 MCs and NMCs appear to receive distinct and complementary patterns of excitatory innervation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the optogenetic circuit mapping data.

claim: L4-specific photo-stimulation drove large EPSCs in NMCs but evoked little to no input in MCs.
source: L4-specific photo-stimulation (with two different stimulus protocols, across four different intensities) drove large EPSCs in NMCs but evoked little to no input in MCs under identical conditions (Figure 2b,c; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on L4-specific optogenetic stimulation experiments shown in figures.

claim: L4 photo-stimulation reliably drove spiking in L5 NMCs, but not in L5 MCs.
source: Current clamp recordings under the same conditions showed that L4 photo-stimulation reliably drove spiking in L5 NMCs, but not in L5 MCs (Figure 2b,d; Figure 2—figure supplement 1) despite the fact that MCs are intrinsically more excitable than NMCs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on L4-specific optogenetic stimulation experiments shown in figures.

claim: MCs are intrinsically more excitable than NMCs.
source: Current clamp recordings under the same conditions showed that L4 photo-stimulation reliably drove spiking in L5 NMCs, but not in L5 MCs (Figure 2b,d; Figure 2—figure supplement 1) despite the fact that MCs are intrinsically more excitable than NMCs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on intrinsic property measurements shown in supplementary figures.

claim: L4 densely innervates and powerfully drives firing in L5 NMCs, but not L5 MCs.
source: Thus, these results indicate a stark difference between L5 NMCs and MCs: L4 densely innervates and powerfully drives firing in L5 NMCs, but not L5 MCs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the L4-specific optogenetic stimulation experiments.

claim: Individual L5 SST cells form inhibitory connections onto L4 PCs or L5 PCs, but not both.
source: These data argue that individual L5 SST cells connect to either L4 PCs or to L5 PCs, but never to both. In other words, L4 PCs and L5 PCs are inhibited by non-overlapping subnetworks of L5 SST cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the 2-photon holographic optogenetic mapping experiments.

claim: L4 PCs and L5 PCs are inhibited by non-overlapping subnetworks of L5 SST cells.
source: These data argue that individual L5 SST cells connect to either L4 PCs or to L5 PCs, but never to both. In other words, L4 PCs and L5 PCs are inhibited by non-overlapping subnetworks of L5 SST cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the 2-photon holographic optogenetic mapping experiments.

claim: No common input locations were detected in n = 10 L4-L5 pairs versus 13.7 ± 5.1% of all input locations in n = 10 L5-L5 pairs (p=1.1 · 10−3).
source: Using this far more conservative test for the detection of common input, we detected no locations in which stimulation evoked common inputs for L4-L5 pairs, whereas we detected at least one common input in 7 of 10 L5-L5 pairs (Figure 3h; no locations in n = 10 L4-L5 pairs versus 13.7 ± 5.1% of all input locations in n = 10 L5-L5 pairs; p=1.1 · 10−3, Wilcoxon rank sum test; see also Figure 3—figure supplement 2k).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the 2-photon holographic optogenetic mapping experiments.

claim: L5 NMC → L4 PC connections were observed in 36/67 pairs tested (54%).
source: We observed extremely frequent L5 NMC → L4 PC connections (36/67 pairs tested; 54%; Figure 4a,b), even across long inter-somatic distances (183 ± 67 µm, mean ±S.D.; Figure 4—figure supplement 1), suggesting that L5 NMCs connect densely onto L4.
evidence: This is a finding from paired recording experiments.

claim: L5 NMCs connect densely onto L4.
source: We observed extremely frequent L5 NMC → L4 PC connections (36/67 pairs tested; 54%; Figure 4a,b), even across long inter-somatic distances (183 ± 67 µm, mean ±S.D.; Figure 4—figure supplement 1), suggesting that L5 NMCs connect densely onto L4.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the paired recording data.

claim: Monosynaptic excitatory connections from L4 PCs to L5 NMCs were observed in 39/72 pairs tested (54%).
source: In the opposite direction, we also frequently observed monosynaptic excitatory connections from L4 PCs onto L5 NMCs, consistent with the optogenetic experiments above (39/72 pairs tested; 54%).
evidence: This is a finding from paired recording experiments.

claim: Excitatory synapses from L4 PCs onto L5 NMCs exhibited profound short-term facilitation during sustained high-frequency firing.
source: These synapses exhibited profound short-term facilitation during sustained high-frequency firing in the presynaptic cell (Figure 4a; Figure 4—figure supplement 3), which is a hallmark of excitatory connections onto SST cells, (Kapfer et al., 2007; Beierlein et al., 2003; Berger et al., 2009) including NMCs (Beierlein et al., 2003; Hu and Agmon, 2016; Tan et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a finding from paired recording experiments, with citations to prior work showing this is a known property.

claim: Reciprocal connections between L4 PCs and L5 NMCs were observed in 23/56 pairs tested (41%).
source: In cases where we tested connectivity bidirectionally, we frequently observed reciprocal connections (23/56 pairs tested; 41%).
evidence: This is a finding from paired recording experiments.

claim: L5 NMCs and L4 PCs form a translaminar feedback inhibitory motif.
source: Thus, L5 NMCs and L4 PCs form a translaminar feedback inhibitory motif.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the paired recording data.

claim: Connections from L5 NMCs onto L4 fast-spiking cells were observed in 12/23 pairs tested (52%).
source: We also observed frequent connections from L5 NMCs onto L4 fast-spiking (FS) cells (12/23 pairs tested; 52%; Figure 4—figure supplement 2), similar to a known circuit in which L4 non-Martinotti SST cells inhibit L4 FS cells (Ma et al., 2006; Xu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a finding from paired recording experiments, with citations to prior work.

claim: Monosynaptic excitatory connections from L4 PCs to L5 MCs were observed in 1/95 pairs tested (1%).
source: In contrast, we almost never observed monosynaptic excitatory connections from L4 PCs to L5 MCs (1/95 pairs tested; 1%; Figure 4a,b) or from L5 MCs onto L4 PCs (4/68 pairs tested; 6%), despite the fact that these pairs were separated by smaller inter-somatic distances than L4 PC - L5 NMC pairs (143 ± 47 µm, mean ±S.D.; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from paired recording experiments.

claim: Connections from L5 MCs onto L4 PCs were observed in 4/68 pairs tested (6%).
source: In contrast, we almost never observed monosynaptic excitatory connections from L4 PCs to L5 MCs (1/95 pairs tested; 1%; Figure 4a,b) or from L5 MCs onto L4 PCs (4/68 pairs tested; 6%), despite the fact that these pairs were separated by smaller inter-somatic distances than L4 PC - L5 NMC pairs (143 ± 47 µm, mean ±S.D.; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from paired recording experiments.

claim: L5 MCs are essentially isolated from the densely interconnected network of L4 PCs and interneurons.
source: These data suggest that L5 NMCs are integrated into the densely interconnected network of L4 PCs and interneurons (Beierlein et al., 2000; Petersen and Sakmann, 2000), whereas L5 MCs are essentially isolated from it.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the paired recording data, with citations to prior work.

claim: Inhibitory connections from L5 MCs onto L5 PCs were observed in 24/46 pairs tested (52%).
source: Indeed, we observed frequent inhibitory connections from L5 MCs onto L5 PCs (24/46 pairs tested; 52%; Figure 4c,d), in agreement with prior literature (Jiang et al., 2015; Fino and Yuste, 2011; Berger et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a finding from paired recording experiments, with citations to prior work.

claim: Excitatory connections from L5 PCs onto L5 MCs were observed in 4/29 pairs tested (14%).
source: We also observed excitatory connections from L5 PCs onto L5 MCs, albeit more rarely (4/29 pairs tested; 14%; Figure 4c,d) but at a rate consistent with the literature (Jiang et al., 2015; Levy and Reyes, 2012).
evidence: This is a finding from paired recording experiments, with citations to prior work.

claim: Inhibitory outputs from L5 NMCs onto L5 PCs were detected in 2/65 pairs tested (3%).
source: In contrast, we detected very few inhibitory outputs from L5 NMCs onto L5 PCs (2/65 pairs tested; 3%; Figure 4c,d) or excitatory connections from L5 PCs onto L5 NMCs (1/60 pairs tested; 2%; Figure 3c,d), despite the fact that L5 PCs were on average located much closer to L5 NMCs than were L4 PCs.
evidence: This is a finding from paired recording experiments.

claim: Excitatory connections from L5 PCs onto L5 NMCs were detected in 1/60 pairs tested (2%).
source: In contrast, we detected very few inhibitory outputs from L5 NMCs onto L5 PCs (2/65 pairs tested; 3%; Figure 4c,d) or excitatory connections from L5 PCs onto L5 NMCs (1/60 pairs tested; 2%; Figure 3c,d), despite the fact that L5 PCs were on average located much closer to L5 NMCs than were L4 PCs.
evidence: This is a finding from paired recording experiments.

claim: The dearth of intralaminar connectivity between L5 PCs and L5 NMCs stands in stark contrast to the dense intralaminar connectivity observed between L5 PCs and L5 MCs.
source: The surprising dearth of intralaminar connectivity between L5 PCs and L5 NMCs stands in stark contrast to the dense intralaminar connectivity observed between L5 PCs and L5 MCs, as well as in other inhibitory circuits (Fino and Yuste, 2011; Packer and Yuste, 2011; Levy and Reyes, 2012).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the paired recording data, with citations to prior work.

claim: MCs and NMCs specifically target L5 PCs and L4 PCs, replicating results from a recent study.
source: Furthermore, our finding that MCs and NMCs specifically target L5 PCs and L4 PCs very closely replicates results from a recent study (Nigro et al., 2018), lending further support to the notion that MCs and NMCs are wired into selective subnetworks with distinct laminar populations.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the paired recording data, with a citation to a recent study.

claim: 87% of TdT+ neurons in X94-ChR2 mice were GFP+.
source: However, most (232/267; 87%) TdT +neurons were GFP+, indicating that CRE-DOG allows expression of ChR2-TdT in GFP +X94 cells with high specificity.
evidence: This is a finding from immunohistochemical analysis of X94-ChR2 mice.

claim: 90% of TdT+ cells in X94-ChR2 mice expressed SST.
source: Furthermore, immunostaining confirmed that the large majority (240/267; 90%) of TdT +cells expressed SST (Figure 5—figure supplement 1d,e).
evidence: This is a finding from immunohistochemical analysis of X94-ChR2 mice.

claim: NMC photostimulation reliably evoked powerful IPSCs in L4 PCs.
source: Consistent with our previous experiments, NMC photostimulation reliably evoked powerful IPSCs in L4 PCs, whereas PCs in other layers usually received small IPSCs or showed no response (mean charge transfer ±C.I: L2/3 = 2.0 ± 1.4 pC; L4 = 10.7 ± 4.8 pC; L5 = 0.8 ± 0.5 pC; L6 = 1.1 ± 0.4 pC).
evidence: This is a finding from slice recording experiments in X94-ChR2 mice.

claim: At the population level, the evoked IPSC was only significant in L4 PCs in X94-ChR2 mice.
source: At the population level, the evoked IPSC was only significant in L4 PCs (L2/3: p=0.41, n = 20; L4: p<10−8, n = 30; L5: p=0.67, n = 27; L6: p=0.84, n = 22; F-test on linear mixed-effects model compared to baseline charge), though a small number of individual L2/3 PCs did exhibit substantial IPSCs.
evidence: This is a finding from slice recording experiments in X94-ChR2 mice.

claim: Photostimulation of X98 cells drove strong inhibition in L2/3 and L5 PCs, but relatively little in L4 and L6 PCs.
source: Slice recordings revealed that photostimulation of these neurons drove strong inhibition in L2/3 and L5 PCs, but relatively little in L4 and L6 PCs (mean charge transfer ±C.I: L2/3 = 33.9 ± 18.7 pC; L4 = 4.7 ± 3.0 pC; L5 = 17.9 ± 5.0 pC; L6 = 4.9 ± 2.7 pC; Figure 5d).
evidence: This is a finding from slice recording experiments in X98-ChR2 mice.

claim: In X98-ChR2 mice, evoked responses at the population level were only significant in L2/3 and L5 PCs.
source: In contrast to X94-ChR2, in X98-ChR2 slices evoked responses at the population level were only significant in L2/3 and L5 PCs (L2/3: p<10−11, n = 6; L4: p=0.46, n = 7; L5: p<10−6, n = 15; L6: p=0.53, n = 4; F-test on linear mixed-effects model).
evidence: This is a finding from slice recording experiments in X98-ChR2 mice.

claim: Photostimulating NMCs powerfully suppressed the spontaneous activity of all units in L4.
source: Recording from X94-ChR2 mice, we observed that photostimulating NMCs powerfully suppressed the spontaneous activity of all units in L4, both FS (Figure 6—figure supplement 2; 5.2 ± 1.7 Hz control versus 1.1 ± 0.5 Hz light; p<10 −6, n = 39 L4 FS units), and RS units (1.8 ± 1.2 Hz control versus 0.9 ± 0.7 Hz light; p<0.001, n = 15 L4 RS units; Figure 6a,b,e,f; Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from in vivo recording experiments in X94-ChR2 mice.

claim: Stimulating NMCs strongly attenuated the response to sensory stimulation in L4 units.
source: Similarly, stimulating NMCs strongly attenuated the response to sensory stimulation in L4 units (L4 RS: 3.8 ± 1.7 Hz control versus 2.3 ± 1.2 Hz light; p<10 −6, n = 15; L4 FS: 7.1 ± 4.0 Hz control versus 2.9 ± 1.0 Hz light; p<10 −6, n = 39; Figure 6c,d,g,h; Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from in vivo recording experiments in X94-ChR2 mice.

claim: Enhancing NMC firing potently suppresses L4 and does not cause a net disinhibition of L4 excitatory neurons.
source: This indicates that, in these conditions, enhancing NMC firing potently suppresses L4 and does not cause a net disinhibition of L4 excitatory neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the in vivo recording data in X94-ChR2 mice.

claim: NMC photostimulation caused little to no change in the activity of the L5 RS and L6 RS populations.
source: NMC photostimulation caused little to no change in the activity of the L5 RS and L6 RS populations (L5 RS spontaneous: 5.1 ± 1.2 Hz control versus 5.1 ± 1.3 Hz light; p=0.20, n = 59; L6 RS spontaneous: 1.9 ± 1.0 Hz control versus 1.6 ± 0.7 Hz light; p=0.42, n = 13; L5 RS sensory-driven: 5.9 ± 1.2 Hz control versus 5.6 ± 1.3 Hz light; p<10 −6, n = 59; L6 RS sensory-driven: 2.1 ± 1.0 Hz control versus 1.9 ± 0.9 Hz light; p=0.04, n = 13), although some individual L5 RS units exhibited substantial increases or decreases in their firing rates.
evidence: This is a finding from in vivo recording experiments in X94-ChR2 mice.

claim: NMC photostimulation robustly reduced spontaneous and sensory-evoked activity in the L2/3 RS population.
source: Although our in vitro data did not reveal a strong monosynaptic connection from NMCs to L2/3 PCS, NMC photostimulation also robustly reduced spontaneous and sensory-evoked activity in the L2/3 RS population (L2/3 RS spontaneous: 0.9 ± 0.5 Hz control versus 0.1 ± 0.1 Hz light; p<10 −4, n = 10; L2/3 sensory-driven: 3.4 ± 1.4 Hz control versus 1.5 ± 0.5 Hz light; p<10 −6, n = 10), as well as that of nearly all FS units, including those outside of L4 (L2/3 FS sensory-driven: 8.3 ± 4.0 Hz control versus 5.6 ± 3.0 Hz light; p<10 −6, n = 11; L5 FS sensory-driven: 7.6 ± 2.8 Hz control versus 4.5 ± 3.0 Hz light; p<10 −6, n = 38; L6 FS sensory-driven: 8.3 ± 3.8 Hz control versus 7.0 ± 4.4 Hz light; p<10 −6, n = 9; Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from in vivo recording experiments in X94-ChR2 mice.

claim: NMC photoactivation indirectly reduces activity in L2/3 by dramatically reducing excitatory input from L4.
source: Because L4 is an important source of excitatory drive to L2/3 PCs and FS cells (Pluta et al., 2015), the most likely explanation is that that NMC photoactivation indirectly reduces activity in L2/3 by dramatically reducing excitatory input from L4.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the in vivo recording data, with a citation to prior work.

claim: Photostimulating SST cells in X98-ChR2 mice substantially reduced the activity of the L2/3 and L5 RS populations during spontaneous conditions.
source: Photostimulating SST cells in X98-ChR2 mice yielded dramatically different effects. The activity of the L2/3 and L5 RS populations was substantially reduced both during spontaneous conditions (L2/3 RS spontaneous: 0.8 ± 0.6 Hz control versus 0.3 ± 0.2 Hz light; p<10 −6, n = 29; L5 RS spontaneous: 5.4 ± 1.5 Hz control versus 4.0 ± 1.8 Hz light; p<10 −6, n = 42; Figure 6a,b,e,f; Figure 6—figure supplement 1), and during sensory stimulation (L2/3 RS sensory-driven: 2.4 ± 0.8 Hz control versus 1.2 ± 0.4 Hz light; p<10 −6, n = 29; L5 RS sensory-driven: 6.4 ± 1.6 Hz control versus 4.5 ± 1.8 Hz light; p<10 −6, n = 42; Figure 6c,d,g,h; Figure 6—figure supplement 1), whereas the activity of the L4 RS population showed no change or small reductions under the same conditions (L4 RS spontaneous: 1.1 ± 0.4 Hz control versus 1.2 ± 0.5 Hz light; p=0.82, n = 12; L4 RS sensory-driven: 2.3 ± 0.8 Hz control versus 2.0 ± 0.6 Hz light; p<0.01, n = 12).
evidence: This is a finding from in vivo recording experiments in X98-ChR2 mice.

claim: X98-ChR2 photostimulation did not cause a significant effect in the L6 RS population.
source: X98-ChR2 photostimulation did not cause a significant effect in the L6 RS population (L6 RS spontaneous: 4.3 ± 4.7 Hz control versus 3.2 ± 2.5 Hz light; p=0.13, n = 6; L6 RS sensory-driven: 4.6 ± 5.0 Hz control versus 4.1 ± 4.1 Hz light; p=0.24, n = 6), though we sampled few L6 units.
evidence: This is a finding from in vivo recording experiments in X98-ChR2 mice.

claim: The activation of SST neurons in X98-ChR2 mice exerts a wholly different effect on the cortical microcircuit than that of SST neurons in X94 mice.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that the activation of SST neurons in X98-ChR2 mice exerts a wholly different effect on the cortical microcircuit than that of SST neurons in X94 mice, which labels NMCs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the in vivo recording data comparing X94-ChR2 and X98-ChR2 mice.

claim: SST subtypes are specialized to modulate specific cortical layers.
source: Furthermore, we did not observe any effect on cortical activity when we repeated these experiments in wild-type mice (injected with the same viral cocktail used with X94/X98 mice), indicating that the effects we observed depended specifically on the optogenetic stimulation of GFP +SST cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1g–j). Two important caveats should be noted in interpreting these results in the context of our L5 MCs circuit mapping data: 1) photostimulation in these experiments activates X98 cells both in L5 and L2/3, and 2) the cells labeled in X98-ChR2 represent a population that is different from the population labeled by the GIN line, which might be expected to exhibit different connectivity (Morishima et al., 2017). However, taken together with our X94-ChR2 data, these results demonstrate that SST subtypes are specialized to modulate specific cortical layers and suggest that MCs and NMCs exert very different effects on cortical activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the in vivo recording data, with a citation to prior work.

claim: MCs and NMCs exert very different effects on cortical activity.
source: Furthermore, we did not observe any effect on cortical activity when we repeated these experiments in wild-type mice (injected with the same viral cocktail used with X94/X98 mice), indicating that the effects we observed depended specifically on the optogenetic stimulation of GFP +SST cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1g–j). Two important caveats should be noted in interpreting these results in the context of our L5 MCs circuit mapping data: 1) photostimulation in these experiments activates X98 cells both in L5 and L2/3, and 2) the cells labeled in X98-ChR2 represent a population that is different from the population labeled by the GIN line, which might be expected to exhibit different connectivity (Morishima et al., 2017). However, taken together with our X94-ChR2 data, these results demonstrate that SST subtypes are specialized to modulate specific cortical layers and suggest that MCs and NMCs exert very different effects on cortical activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the in vivo recording data.

claim: Clustering tdTomato+ and GFP+/tdTomato+ cells together based on the 1000 top variable genes yielded 10 distinguishable clusters of SST+ neurons.
source: Clustering tdTomato+ and GFP+/ tdTomato+ cells together based on the 1000 top variable genes yielded 10 distinguishable clusters of SST+ neurons (Figure 7a).
evidence: This is a finding from single-cell RNA sequencing analysis.

claim: These clusters showed remarkable correspondence to clusters similarly generated from single-cell RNA-seq on SST+ neurons from primary visual cortex (V1sp) and anterior lateral motor cortex (ALM).
source: These clusters showed remarkable correspondence to clusters similarly generated from single-cell RNA-seq on SST+ neurons from primary visual cortex (V1sp) and anterior lateral motor cortex (ALM) (Figure 7—figure supplement 1), supporting the idea that SST cell types are conserved across cortical regions (Tasic et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a finding from single-cell RNA sequencing analysis, with a citation to prior work.

claim: ~84% (157 out of 188) GFP+/SST+ neurons were distributed among three clusters.
source: We then asked whether single-cell RNA-seq could distinguish X94-GFP+ cells. Indeed,~84% (157 out of 188) GFP+/SST+ neurons were distributed among three clusters, with just over half of all GFP cells (102 cells) falling within a single cluster (cluster m10) that could be defined by the specific expression of the gene Hpse (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is a finding from single-cell RNA sequencing analysis.

claim: Just over half of all GFP cells (102 cells) fell within a single cluster (cluster m10) that could be defined by the specific expression of the gene Hpse.
source: We then asked whether single-cell RNA-seq could distinguish X94-GFP+ cells. Indeed,~84% (157 out of 188) GFP+/SST+ neurons were distributed among three clusters, with just over half of all GFP cells (102 cells) falling within a single cluster (cluster m10) that could be defined by the specific expression of the gene Hpse (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is a finding from single-cell RNA sequencing analysis.

claim: The co-localization of Hpse expression in ~67% of GFP/tdTomato-positive cells validates the assignment of ~half of X94-GFP cells to cluster m10 based on single-cell RNA-seq.
source: The co-localization of Hpse expression in ~67% of GFP/tdTomato-positive cells validates the assignment of ~half of X94-GFP cells to cluster m10 based on single-cell RNA-seq.
evidence: This is a finding from RNA in situ hybridization experiments validating the single-cell RNA sequencing results.

claim: Hpse labels SST-cre;tdTomato+ cells found primarily within L4 and L5, similar to the laminar distribution of X94 cells.
source: Notably, Hpse – a marker for the cluster m10, the main X94-GFP-containing cluster – labels SST-cre;tdTomato+ cells found primarily within L4 and L5, similar to the laminar distribution of X94 cells.
evidence: This is a finding from RNA in situ hybridization experiments.

claim: Hpse defines the L4/L5 NMC cells.
source: Taken together, these data strongly suggest that Hpse defines the L4/L5 NMC cells, and further support the idea that the transcriptomically defined SST neurons described here represent biologically meaningful sub-classes with distinct characteristics based on their anatomy, morphology, connectivity and physiology.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the single-cell RNA sequencing and RNA in situ hybridization data.

claim: The transcriptomically defined SST neurons represent biologically meaningful sub-classes with distinct characteristics based on their anatomy, morphology, connectivity and physiology.
